choices.text: Speculative decoding is an inference technique designed to accelerate large language model (LLM) generation by exploiting a smaller, faster "draft" model to propose candidate tokens that a larger "target" model can verify in a single forward pass. The core intuition is that autoregressive decoding is often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth rather than compute: the target model must load its enormous weights and KV cache for every token, even though the arithmetic per token is modest. By letting a compact draft model generate a sequence of k candidate tokens (a "draft" or "speculation") with its own lightweight weights, the target model can then evaluate all k tokens in one parallel step using its full attention mechanism, because the draft tokens are known and can be appended to the context. This transforms k sequential target-model passes into a single one, provided the draft's predictions are frequently correct. The verification step uses the target model's own logits over the draft tokens; if a token matches the target's top prediction (or falls within an accepted distribution), it is kept, otherwise decoding stops at the first mismatch and the correct token from the target model is emitted. This accept/reject logic preserves the exact output distribution of the target model, meaning speculative decoding is lossless with respect to generation quality.
